claims.subject: work:wimmer_glick_schiller_2002
claims.statement: Wimmer and Glick Schiller question the treatment of nation, state and society as naturally coincident units of analysis.
claims.qualification: A jointly authored methodological critique of dominant social-science tendencies; it does not assert that every earlier historian used a national container.
claims.locator: Published pp. 301–303, introduction and Three modes of methodological nationalism

claims.subject: work:wimmer_glick_schiller_2002
claims.statement: Wimmer and Glick Schiller argue that studying transnational communities can reproduce boundedness and obscure differences of class, gender and power.
claims.qualification: Selected pp. 324–325 only; transnational research is not automatically free from the assumptions it criticizes. No universal rejection of community research inferred.
claims.locator: Published pp. 324–325, transnational communities and Some final remarks

claims.subject: work:brubaker_diaspora_2005
claims.statement: Brubaker proposes studying diaspora as an idiom, stance and claim instead of assuming a bounded collective entity.
claims.qualification: Author abstract only; one intervention in a contested interdisciplinary debate, not a settled definition of every diaspora.

claims.subject: work:brubaker_diaspora_2005
claims.statement: Brubaker examines the expanding uses of diaspora and questions claims that this expansion demonstrates a wholly new social world.
claims.qualification: Author abstract only; neither all migration nor every cross-border connection becomes diaspora through this argument.

claims.subject: work:mckeown_regionalization_2007
claims.statement: McKeown argues that growing global integration of migration accompanied increasing regional segregation.
claims.qualification: Selected opening of the 2007 conference paper; the argument concerns historical migration systems, not a claim that borders disappeared. Statistical estimates have not been independently reproduced.
claims.locator: PDF pp. 1–3, opening before Memories of Migration

claims.subject: work:mckeown_regionalization_2007
claims.statement: McKeown challenges histories that make Atlantic migration the norm and treat Asian movement as inherently different or external to globalization.
claims.qualification: Selected pp. 2–7; preserve differences in coercion, routes and political intervention. Counts include repeated journeys and have gaps; they are not counts of unique migrants.
claims.locator: PDF pp. 2–7, opening, Memories of Migration and start of Long Distance Migration

claims.subject: work:greefs_winter_2024
claims.statement: Greefs and Winter connect longer migration distances with declining selection by class and gender in their study of Antwerp-bound migrants.
claims.qualification: An Antwerp case for 1850–1910; democratization describes changing access to long-distance movement, not equal rights or a universal global trajectory.
claims.locator: Published pp. 383–386, introduction and Migration selectivity and the mobility transition

claims.subject: work:greefs_winter_2024
claims.statement: Greefs and Winter combine spatial and social analysis of foreigners’ files to examine changes in migration trajectories.
claims.qualification: Selected source discussion only; police-produced classifications and recorded foreign newcomers delimit the sample. No independent reproduction of their quantitative results or inference about every unrecorded migrant.
claims.locator: Published pp. 386–387, Case study and sources

claims.subject: work:reinecke_loehr_2024
claims.statement: Reinecke and Löhr distinguish deep-history, genealogical and contrapuntal ways of relating past migration to the present.
claims.qualification: The coauthors’ analytical proposal, not a classification of all historians or an assertion that these modes began in 2024.

claims.subject: work:reinecke_loehr_2024
claims.statement: Reinecke and Löhr propose using historical alternatives and ruptures to unsettle apparently inevitable categories of migration and belonging.
claims.qualification: Selected introduction and section 3; past alternatives do not erase enduring colonial inequalities. Their cited scholars’ works have not thereby been read independently.

claims.subject: work:liebisch_guemues_mobilities
claims.statement: Liebisch-Gümüş describes mobility history as a heterogeneous area spanning transportation, migration, tourism, environmental and global histories.
claims.qualification: English version 2, selected section 1. This is her assessment, not evidence that all historians adopted one new paradigm or that mobility is synonymous with migration.
claims.locator: Section 1, What is the History of Mobility?, lines 24–42

claims.subject: work:liebisch_guemues_mobilities
claims.statement: Liebisch-Gümüş stresses unequal access, forced settlement and immobility when questioning narratives of continually increasing movement.
claims.qualification: English version 2, selected section 2. Mobility is spatial here; it is not automatically social ascent. No new 2024 origin asserted for the surveyed arguments.
claims.locator: Section 2, Increased Mobility as a Sign of Contemporary History?, lines 49–76

prior_work_annotations.attribution_note: Description-supported lead retained; no new body reading or practitioner promotion.
Twelve credited forum authors. The opening is the only substantive passage checked; individual essays and author-specific arguments remain unread. Metadata credit is not collective assent.

boundary_review.review_note: Navigation and teaching distinctions are editorial proposals, not historical influence relationships.

decisions.rationale: Expose the methodological problem of borders, connections and national categories without absorbing all global or migration history.
Existing Atlantic migration strands are geographically insufficient for the Asian and comparative questions documented here; internal migration also requires review.
Review as a cross-field approach including transport, infrastructure, unequal access and immobility. Dedicated-entry status is not decided by one survey.
Preserve Atlantic/African diaspora strands and Lovejoy context while investigating diasporas elsewhere. Brubaker alone cannot determine the boundaries or displace historical actors’ categories.

transnational.label: Transnational history
transnational.description: Historical approaches examining connections across political and social boundaries and the making of those boundaries. Selected interventions question national units, unequal circulation and the historical categories used to describe movement.
transnational.scope_note: Provisional separate teaching entry for an approach with multiple histories, not a unified school. Global, international, connected, borderlands, migration, mobility and diaspora histories overlap without being interchangeable. Earlier roots and regional traditions need further review.
